purpose: Prednisone is used to reduce inflammation and calm down an overactive immune system. It can treat a wide range of conditions including allergic reactions, asthma, arthritis, skin problems, and certain autoimmune diseases. Doctors also use it to help prevent organ rejection after a transplant.
how_it_works: Your immune system sometimes goes into overdrive and causes swelling, redness, and pain. Prednisone works by mimicking a natural hormone your body already makes called cortisol, which helps dial down that overactive immune response. Think of it like a volume knob that turns down the inflammation in your body.
common_side_effects: Increased appetite and weight gain, trouble sleeping, mood changes or feeling more emotional, increased blood sugar levels, upset stomach, acne, and puffy or rounded face. With long-term use, you may also notice weaker bones or muscles.
warnings: Do not stop taking prednisone suddenly without talking to your doctor — your body needs time to adjust, so the dose must be slowly reduced. It can raise your blood sugar, so diabetic patients need to monitor closely. It can also lower your ability to fight infections, so avoid contact with sick people. Tell your doctor if you have a history of stomach ulcers, high blood pressure, glaucoma, or osteoporosis.
typical_dosing: Dosing varies a lot depending on what condition is being treated. It can range from 5 mg to 60 mg or more per day, taken by mouth, usually once in the morning with food to reduce stomach upset. Your doctor will often start you on a higher dose and gradually taper it down as your condition improves.
